title: Knot tying: one-handed reef knot, surgeon's knot and instrument tie

guidelineVersions: Intercollegiate Basic Surgical Skills course programme, 7th ed. (RCS England 2025)

related.id: MB-180 Interrupted suturing and wound closure
related.why: Instrument ties in use on a skin wound
Holding the needle holder and scissors

brief.scenario: You have a knot-tying board with a tube to ligate, a braided suture, a monofilament suture on a needle, a needle holder, artery forceps and scissors.
brief.task: Tie a one-handed reef knot and a surgeon's knot, then an instrument tie. Ligate the tube at depth. Explain the principles of a secure knot as you go.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Square every throw, lay it flat, tension in line with the tissue, and keep the needle safe.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Throwing in the same direction twice, which makes a slipping granny knot.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "I'll identify the short and long ends and keep equal, opposite tension."

grid.label: Set-up and handling
grid.fail: Starts without identifying the ends, or grips the working length of suture in an instrument.
grid.pass: Identifies short and long ends; positions hands and board; instruments grasp only the short tail.
grid.high: States which knot suits the task (tension, depth, material) before tying.

grid.label: One-handed reef knot
grid.fail: Repeats the same throw, making a granny knot that slips.
grid.pass: Alternates each throw; crosses hands so the knot lies flat and square.
grid.high: Ties smoothly with either hand leading, laying each throw down with the index finger.

grid.label: Surgeon's knot
grid.fail: Lets the first throw loosen before the second is placed.
grid.pass: Double wrap on the first throw holds under tension; then a single throw in the opposite direction squares it.
grid.high: Uses it where tissue is under tension, accepting the extra bulk.

grid.label: Instrument tie
grid.fail: Wraps the same way each time, or crushes the suture in the jaws.
grid.pass: Wraps the long end round the needle holder, grasps only the short tail, alternates wrap direction, and crosses the hands.
grid.high: Keeps the needle holder close to the knot and short tails, saving suture and time.

grid.label: Tension and tying at depth
grid.fail: Leaves an air knot, saws the strands, or lifts the tube while tightening.
grid.pass: Equal, opposite tension in one plane; index finger carries each throw down onto the tube; snug without strangling.
grid.high: At depth, keeps tension in line with the vessel, pushing down rather than pulling up, so the tie cannot avulse it.

grid.label: Cutting and sharps
grid.fail: Cuts into the knot, or leaves the needle loose on the field.
grid.pass: Checks the knot, then cuts with the scissor tips in view, leaving short tails; needle kept on the holder, then into the sharps bin.
grid.high: Leaves longer tails on monofilament, which unties more easily.

grid.label: Principles of knot security
grid.fail: Cannot distinguish a reef knot from a granny knot.
grid.pass: Square knot holds; granny slips; monofilament needs more throws than braided; beyond that, extra throws add bulk, not strength.
grid.high: Security depends on material, configuration and technique; follows the manufacturer's advice for each suture.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: [Picks up the suture and starts tying without identifying the ends.]

fail.text: [One-handed: two throws in the same direction.] That's a reef knot.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: [Surgeon's knot: first throw slackens while reaching for the second.]

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: [Instrument tie: grips the long strand in the needle holder jaws; same wrap twice.]

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: [At depth: pulls the tube upwards as he tightens; knot sits loose above it.]

fail.speaker: candidate

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Examiner: "What's the difference between a reef knot and a granny knot?"

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I don't think there is one really, as long as it's tight.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Short end on the left, long end in my right hand. I'll only put instruments on the tail.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: [One-handed reef knot: first throw, crosses hands; second throw in the opposite direction.] Each throw is opposite to the last, so it lies flat.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: [Surgeon's knot: double wrap first, holds, then a single throw the other way.] The double wrap holds against tension.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: [Instrument tie: long end wrapped round the needle holder, grasps the short tail, pulls through; next wrap the opposite way.]

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: [Ties round the tube at depth, index finger taking each throw down; equal, opposite pull.] Snug, not strangling.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: [Checks the knot; cuts with tips visible, short tails; needle into the sharps bin.]

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Square throws: a granny slips. Monofilament is slippery, so it needs more throws than braided. Extra throws add bulk, not strength.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'll use the braided tie for the ligature and the monofilament for the instrument tie. Short end left, long end right; instruments only on the tail.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: [One-handed reef knot, left hand then right leading, index finger laying each throw flat.] Alternating throws keep it square.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: [Surgeon's knot.] I'd use this where the tissue is under tension. The double first throw holds while I place the second; the cost is a bulkier knot.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: [Instrument tie with the needle holder kept close to the knot, alternating wraps, hands crossing each time.] Staying close saves suture.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: [At depth: finger pushes each throw down in line with the tube, never lifting it.] Pulling up on a deep vessel can avulse it.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: [Checks the knot, then cuts with tips visible.] I'll leave the monofilament tails a little longer, as it unties more easily. [Needle straight into the sharps bin.]

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Material, configuration and technique. Square throws laid flat; a granny slips. Monofilament needs more throws than braided, and I follow the manufacturer's advice for each suture. Extra throws only add bulk.

failures.move: Two throws in the same direction.
failures.consequence: A granny knot, which slips: a ligature can come off a vessel.

failures.move: Pulling upwards while tying at depth.
failures.consequence: Safety-critical: can tear or avulse the vessel being tied.

failures.move: Leaving the needle loose on the field.
failures.consequence: Safety-critical: needlestick risk to the operator and team.

failures.move: Grasping the working length of suture in the needle holder jaws.
failures.consequence: Crushes and weakens the suture, which may break.

recovery.line: That's become a granny knot. I'll take it down and square the throws.
I'll use a surgeon's knot, with a double first throw, to hold the tension.

knowledge.fact: Reef (square) knot: two throws in opposite directions, lying flat. Granny knot: two throws in the same direction; it slips.
Surgeon's knot: double wrap on the first throw, which resists slipping under tension, then a square throw.
Instrument ties and tying at depth are core skills of the Basic Surgical Skills course.
Monofilament holds knots less well than braided; once a square knot has enough throws for the material, extra throws add bulk rather than strength.

recall.think: A slipping ligature on a vessel bleeds.
recall.say: "Each throw opposite to the last, laid flat."
do: Identify ends; instruments on the tail only
Square every throw; equal, opposite tension
At depth push down, never pull up

numbers.meaning: on the first throw of a surgeon's knot

recall.trap: A tight granny knot looks secure but slips.
recall.finish: Check, cut with tips visible, needle to the sharps bin.

partner.opening: Here is the knot-tying board. Please tie a one-handed reef knot and a surgeon's knot, then an instrument tie, and ligate the tube at depth, explaining as you go.

reveals.finding: Watch whether the candidate identifies the short and long ends and where instruments are placed.
Tug the knot: it should not slip. Look for flat, alternating throws.
Check that the jaws hold only the short tail and that the wrap direction alternates.
Watch the direction of pull: down along the tube, not up.

push.question: Why did that knot slip?
push.expect: Both throws went in the same direction, making a granny knot; alternate the throws to square it.

push.question: When would you use a surgeon's knot?
push.expect: Where the tissue is under tension: the double first throw stops it loosening before the second throw.

push.question: Does a monofilament need the same number of throws as a braided suture?
push.expect: No: monofilament holds knots less well, so it needs more throws; follow the manufacturer's advice.

curveballs.prompt: "Tie the knot one-handed with your non-dominant hand."
curveballs.safeAnswer: Ties with the other hand leading, still alternating throws and crossing hands so it lies flat.

curveballs.prompt: "The tie breaks as you tighten it at depth."
curveballs.safeAnswer: Control the vessel (pressure or clamp), then re-tie with steady, in-line tension, not a jerk.
It can be slid down to snug a tie, but it must then be locked with square throws, or it will slip.
